exam.title: Mathematics I - Exam B
exam.subtitle: Algebra, Induction and Linear Algebra
exam.instructions: Complete all tasks and show your work. Permitted aids: non-programmable calculator.

exercises.title: Sum formula and divisibility
exercises.description:
a) Prove by induction: $\sum_{k=1}^n k(k+1) = \frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{3}$.
b) Prove: $7 \mid 8^n - 1$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Base case
$n = 1$: left $1\cdot2 = 2$, right $\frac{1\cdot2\cdot3}{3} = 2$ ✓.

Step 2: Part a): Induction step
Let the formula be true for $n$ (IH). Then $\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}k(k+1) = \frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{3} + (n+1)(n+2) = \frac{(n+1)(n+2)\,(n + 3)}{3}$, since $\frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{3} + (n+1)(n+2) = (n+1)(n+2)\left(\frac n3 + 1\right)$. This is the claim for $n+1$.

Step 3: Part b): Base and hypothesis
$n = 1$: $8 - 1 = 7$ ✓. IH: $8^n - 1 = 7m$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$.

exercises.title: Irreducibility over 𝔽₂ and ℝ
exercises.description:
a) Show that $x^3 + x + 1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{F}_2$.
b) Factor $x^4 + 1$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$.
c) Factor $x^4 + 1$ over $\mathbb{R}$ into quadratic factors.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Root test
A polynomial of degree $3$ is reducible over a field exactly when it has a root (a linear factor would split off). $f(0) = 1$, $f(1) = 1 + 1 + 1 = 1$ in $\mathbb{F}_2$. No root: $f$ is irreducible.

Step 2: Part b): Frobenius trick
In characteristic $2$ we have $(x+1)^2 = x^2 + 2x + 1 = x^2 + 1$, so $(x+1)^4 = (x^2+1)^2 = x^4 + 1$. Hence $x^4 + 1 = (x+1)^4$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$.

Step 3: Part c): Completing the square
$x^4 + 1 = (x^2 + 1)^2 - 2x^2 = (x^2 + 1)^2 - (\sqrt2x)^2$. Third binomial formula: $x^4 + 1 = (x^2 + \sqrt2x + 1)(x^2 - \sqrt2x + 1)$.

Step 4: Part c): Irreducibility of the factors
The discriminant $2 - 4 = -2 < 0$ shows that the quadratic factors have no roots over $\mathbb{R}$. Check by expanding: $(x^2+1)^2 - 2x^2 = x^4 + 2x^2 + 1 - 2x^2 = x^4 + 1$ ✓.

exercises.title: Eigenvalues, eigenvectors and power
exercises.description:
Let $A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$.
a) Determine eigenvalues and eigenvectors.
b) Compute $A^3$ using diagonalisation.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Eigenvalues
$\operatorname{tr}A = 7$, $\det A = 10$: $\lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10 = (\lambda-2)(\lambda-5) = 0$, so $\lambda_1 = 5$, $\lambda_2 = 2$.

Step 2: Part a): Eigenvectors
$\lambda = 5$: $A - 5I = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$ gives $v = (1,1)^T$. $\lambda = 2$: $A - 2I = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ gives $v = (1,-2)^T$.

Step 3: Part b): Diagonalisation
$P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$, $D = \operatorname{diag}(5,2)$, $\det P = -3$, $P^{-1} = \frac13\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$.

Step 4: Part b): Power
$D^3 = \operatorname{diag}(125,8)$. $PD^3 = \begin{pmatrix} 125 & 8 \\ 125 & -16 \end{pmatrix}$. $A^3 = PD^3P^{-1} = \frac13\begin{pmatrix} 125 & 8 \\ 125 & -16 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} = \frac13\begin{pmatrix} 258 & 117 \\ 234 & 141 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 86 & 39 \\ 78 & 47 \end{pmatrix}$.

Step 5: Check
Directly: $A^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 18 & 7 \\ 14 & 11 \end{pmatrix}$, $A^3 = A^2A = \begin{pmatrix} 72+14 & 18+21 \\ 56+22 & 14+33 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 86 & 39 \\ 78 & 47 \end{pmatrix}$ ✓.

exercises.title: Span, basis and membership
exercises.description:
Let $W = \operatorname{span}\{(1,1,0),(0,1,1),(1,2,1)\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$.
a) Determine a basis and $\dim W$.
b) Does $(1,0,-1)$ lie in $W$?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Spot the dependence
$(1,1,0) + (0,1,1) = (1,2,1)$. The third vector is the sum of the first two and can be omitted.

Step 2: Part a): Basis
$(1,1,0)$ and $(0,1,1)$ are not proportional, hence linearly independent. Basis $\{(1,1,0),(0,1,1)\}$, $\dim W = 2$.

Step 3: Part b): Set-up
$a(1,1,0) + b(0,1,1) = (a,\ a + b,\ b) \overset{!}{=} (1,0,-1)$. From the first and third component $a = 1$, $b = -1$.

Step 4: Part b): Check of the second component
$a + b = 0$ ✓ agrees with $0$. So $(1,0,-1) = (1,1,0) - (0,1,1) \in W$.

Step 5: Counterexample for orientation
$(1,0,0) \notin W$: from $a = 1$, $b = 0$ we get $a + b = 1 \neq 0$. Remember: $W$ is the plane $\{(x,y,z) \mid y = x + z\}$; for $(1,0,-1)$: $0 = 1 - 1$ ✓.

exercises.title: Congruences and remainder theorem
exercises.description:
a) Solve $x \equiv 2 \pmod 3$, $x \equiv 3 \pmod 5$.
b) Compute $3^{100} \bmod 7$.
c) Determine the inverse of $4$ modulo $9$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Set-up
The moduli $3$ and $5$ are coprime, so by the Chinese remainder theorem a solution exists modulo $15$. From the second congruence $x = 3 + 5k$.

Step 2: Part a): Substituting
$3 + 5k \equiv 2 \pmod 3 \iff 2k \equiv -1 \equiv 2 \pmod 3 \iff k \equiv 1 \pmod 3$. So $x = 3 + 5(1 + 3m) = 8 + 15m$, i.e. $x \equiv 8 \pmod{15}$. Check: $8 = 2\cdot3 + 2$ ✓, $8 = 1\cdot5 + 3$ ✓.

Step 3: Part b): Fermat's little theorem
$3^6 \equiv 1 \pmod 7$. Since $100 = 16\cdot6 + 4$: $3^{100} = (3^6)^{16}\cdot3^4 \equiv 3^4 = 81 = 11\cdot7 + 4 \equiv 4 \pmod 7$.

Step 4: Part c): Inverse
$\gcd(4,9) = 1$. By trial or Euclid: $9 = 2\cdot4 + 1 \Rightarrow 1 = 9 - 2\cdot4$, so $4^{-1} \equiv -2 \equiv 7 \pmod 9$. Check: $4\cdot7 = 28 = 3\cdot9 + 1$ ✓.

exercises.title: Difference operator on polynomials
exercises.description:
Let $P_2$ be the space of polynomials of degree $\leq 2$ and $T: P_2 \to P_2$, $(Tp)(x) = p(x+1) - p(x)$.
a) Show that $T$ is linear.
b) Determine the matrix with respect to the basis $\{1,x,x^2\}$.
c) Determine $\ker T$, $\operatorname{im} T$ and show $T^3 = 0$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Linearity
$T(p + q)(x) = (p+q)(x+1) - (p+q)(x) = (p(x+1) - p(x)) + (q(x+1) - q(x)) = Tp + Tq$ and $T(\lambda p) = \lambda Tp$ analogously. Moreover $Tp$ again has degree $\leq 2$ (in fact $\leq \deg p - 1$).

Step 2: Part b): Images of the basis
$T(1) = 1 - 1 = 0$, $T(x) = (x+1) - x = 1$, $T(x^2) = (x+1)^2 - x^2 = 2x + 1$.

Step 3: Part b): Matrix
Coordinates with respect to $(1,x,x^2)$ as columns: $T(1) \to (0,0,0)$, $T(x) \to (1,0,0)$, $T(x^2) \to (1,2,0)$. $[T] = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$.

Step 4: Part c): Kernel and image
$\ker T$: $a + bx + cx^2 \mapsto b + c + 2cx = 0 \iff c = 0, b = 0$. So $\ker T = \{\text{constants}\} = \operatorname{span}\{1\}$. $\operatorname{im} T = \operatorname{span}\{1, 2x+1\} = P_1$ (dimension $2$). Rank–nullity: $1 + 2 = 3$ ✓.

Step 5: Part c): Nilpotency
$[T]^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and $[T]^3 = 0$ (strictly upper triangular matrix). Intuitively: $T$ lowers the degree by $1$; applied three times every polynomial of degree $\leq 2$ becomes $0$.
